v: In eighteen eighty-one, Ottawa started renting out prairie grass for one cent an acre.
That cheap grass helped turn a police fort on the Bow River into a cattle town.
This is Calgary Origins, episode two. The ranch era.
To understand it, start with what disappeared first.
Glenbow's history of the Blackfoot says the buffalo disappeared from the Canadian prairies in eighteen seventy-nine. By eighteen eighty, they were gone.
For the Blackfoot peoples, who had lived on the buffalo, the loss was enormous. Glenbow records that many people starved.
Cattle were already trickling in. In the fall of eighteen seventy-four, a man named Shaw drove five hundred beef cattle across the mountains from British Columbia.
He stayed, at the urging of the Reverend John McDougall. The McDougalls kept their own herd near their mission at Morleyville, today's Morley.
In eighteen seventy-five, Joe McFarland and Henry Olsen arrived from Montana with a herd of dairy cattle.
Then Ottawa made it big business. On May twentieth, eighteen eighty-one, an order in council set out the rules for grazing leases.
One lease could cover up to one hundred thousand acres. It could run for twenty-one years. And the rent was one cent an acre.
The first big player was a senator from Montreal, Matthew Cochrane.
In eighteen eighty-one, he launched what is recognized as Alberta's first large-scale ranch, the Cochrane Ranche, on land west of Calgary.
Its headquarters sat in a sheltered valley on Big Hill Creek, near today's town of Cochrane.
Others followed in eighteen eighty-two. To the south, the Oxley Ranch secured a lease of two hundred thousand acres.
East of Calgary, an army officer, Thomas Bland Strange, took a ranching lease to raise cavalry horses for the British army.
On paper, it looked like an easy fortune. The grass was cheap. The cattle were coming.
Would you have bet on cattle here? Yes or no?
Alberta's first big ranch lost thousands of cattle in just two winters.
In eighteen eighty-one, the Cochrane Ranche bought its herd in Montana.
A trading firm from Fort Benton, Montana, was contracted to drive the cattle north.
The main herd numbered six or seven thousand head, at sixteen dollars a head, delivered at the border.
The drivers pushed hard. Steers covered fifteen to eighteen miles a day.
Then winter came. In the winter of eighteen eighty-one to eighty-two, losses were heavy: close to a thousand head, by one account.
In eighteen eighty-two, a second herd arrived: four thousand, two hundred and ninety head, on October nineteenth.
The next winter was worse. By one count, the Cochrane Ranche lost at least three thousand head.
A letter in eighteen eighty-three said: our losses are enormous.
In eighteen eighty-three, the company moved its cattle south, to a new lease on the Belly River.
The original Cochrane land turned to horses and sheep, under a new name: the British American Ranch Company.
Meanwhile, southwest of Calgary, another outfit was taking shape.
In June eighteen eighty-one, Fred Stimson, from Quebec, began organizing the North-West Cattle Company, backed by the Allan family of Montreal.
It was chartered in March eighteen eighty-two. Its ranch on Pekisko Creek became known by its brand: the Bar U.
Stimson bought more than three thousand cattle in Idaho, and drove them to the company's lease west of High River.
By eighteen ninety, the Bar U was among the largest ranches in Canada: nearly one hundred and fifty-eight thousand acres of leased land, and more than ten thousand head of cattle.
Today, Parks Canada protects the Bar U as a national historic site, for its role in Canada's ranching story.
One of its horse-breakers, says the Canadian Encyclopedia, was Harry Longabaugh, better known as the Sundance Kid.
Cochrane or the Bar U: which ranch would you have ridden for?
Calgary's first millionaire built his fortune on beef.
But first, the railway.
The Canadian Pacific Railway reached Calgary in eighteen eighty-three.
Calgary became the distributing and shipping point for the ranch country around it.
Live cattle went to London, Liverpool and Glasgow. Until the turn of the twentieth century, that trade mattered more to Canada than wheat.
In eighteen eighty-six, the Calgary District and Agricultural Society held the first exhibition, in a town of about a thousand people.
Then came Patrick Burns.
In eighteen eighty-seven, contractors William Mackenzie and Donald Mann hired him to supply meat to their construction camps.
In eighteen ninety, he built his first slaughterhouse, on the east side of the Elbow River in Calgary.
The plant burned down in eighteen ninety-two. The business kept growing.
By nineteen oh two, he was called the beef king of the West.
In nineteen oh five, he incorporated his packing houses as one company. It went on to run plants in Edmonton, Vancouver, Regina, Winnipeg and even Seattle.
The Canadian Encyclopedia calls him the city's first millionaire, and his company the largest integrated meat business in Canada.
He was a rancher too. By the First World War, he controlled more than four hundred thousand acres, and more than thirty thousand head of cattle.
In nineteen oh two, he bought the Bow Valley Ranch, now inside Fish Creek Provincial Park.
Other ranchers built Calgary too. Alfred Ernest Cross started the A Seven ranch in eighteen eighty-five, on Mosquito Creek, west of Nanton.
In eighteen ninety-two, he founded the Calgary Brewing and Malting Company.
His house in east Calgary, built in eighteen ninety-one, is a provincial historic resource today.
And in eighteen ninety-one, the Ranchmen's Club was founded in Calgary, largely based on the Saint James Club in Montreal.
Did you know Calgary's first millionaire was a meat packer? Yes or no?
One winter, the chinook never came.
But the open range was already shrinking.
In eighteen ninety-two, ranchers got four years' notice: the old leases that kept homesteaders out would be cancelled.
Settlers arrived to farm. A Parks Canada plaque says pressure from farmers and smaller ranchers reduced the large ranges.
Ranchers organized. In eighteen ninety-six, cattlemen met at Macleod, now Fort Macleod, and formed the Western Stock Growers' Association.
At the Bar U, a new boss took over. George Lane had come as foreman in eighteen eighty-four.
In nineteen oh two, he and his partners bought the ranch, for two hundred and twenty thousand dollars.
Lane built up what his biography calls the largest pure-bred Percheron stud in the world.
Then came the winter of nineteen oh six to oh seven. The usual chinook never came.
Stock losses ran into the thousands.
Parks Canada's plaque says that hard winter marked the end of the era of the big ranches.
Before then, says the Canadian Encyclopedia, the open-range cattle industry was Calgary's dominant economic activity.
But the ranchers had one more idea.
In nineteen twelve, four of them, Pat Burns, Alfred Ernest Cross, George Lane and Archibald McLean, guaranteed one hundred thousand dollars to stage the first Calgary Stampede.
It ran from September second to fifth, nineteen twelve.
Downtown, the Burns Building, home to one of his retail meat markets, went up in nineteen twelve and nineteen thirteen. It still stands, a provincial historic resource.

In nineteen thirty-one, at a huge celebration of Burns' approaching seventy-fifth birthday, a three-thousand-pound cake was shared with some fifteen thousand people. That day, he was named to the Senate.
The ranch era was short. But the Stampede those ranchers backed is still going.
Is Calgary still a cattle town at heart? Yes or no?
